title: Choosing the Appropriate Preparation and Technique for the Advanced Characterization of Nuclear Fuels and Materials
content: The state of the art for characterization, imaging, and testing of nuclear fuels and materials is evolving with the broader microscopy field. The characterization of radiation damage at the microstructure level has grown beyond the reference texts of Williams and Carter [1] and Jenkins and Kirk [2] with advances in sample preparation techniques (e.g., 3 mm electropolished disk vs. focused ion beam [FIB]-produced lamella) and instrumentation (e.g., conventional transmission electron microscopy [TEM] vs. scanning TEM [STEM] vs. atom probe tomography [APT], and others). However, each technique has associated benefits, drawbacks, costs, and limitations, requiring the integration of multiple techniques to achieve a holistic view of the irradiated microstructure to access fundamental insights. Thus, the question becomes when insights from a newer technique are more applicable than those of traditional techniques. The objective of this work is to discuss benefits and drawbacks of common techniques to study radiation damage, with a focus on delivering the most impact per measurement. Case studies from Oak Ridge National Laboratory are used to characterize (1) black spots and dislocation loops, (2) clustering and precipitates, and (3) cavities.
